parts.description: A smooth white glazed ceramic bowl with a rounded body, rolled rim, and small raised foot ring. The surface is hard, glossy, and slightly off-white porcelain or stoneware.
parts.reasoning: The object appears to be a medium household ceramic bowl with a concave open interior, thick rolled rim, rounded exterior wall, and small circular foot. No exact product dimensions are provided, so typical dimensions are estimated at roughly 0.14-0.16 m rim diameter, 0.07-0.09 m height, 0.055-0.075 m foot diameter, and 3-5 mm wall thickness. Glazed porcelain/stoneware has a true material density around 2200-2500 kg/m^3; using about 2300 kg/m^3 and an estimated ceramic shell volume of 1.6e-4 to 2.0e-4 m^3 gives a mass near 0.37-0.46 kg, so 0.42 kg is a reasonable rigid-body mass. The root density is set to the dominant ceramic material density rather than the hollow bounding-box density, because this is the correct USD/PhysX material-density interpretation when computing mass from collision volume. The dominant contact material is glazed ceramic: it is hard and smooth, with moderate friction on typical lab/table surfaces. Static friction is estimated at 0.45 and dynamic friction at 0.35; values can be lower on polished glass or metal and higher on rubber mats. Restitution is set to 0.50: ceramic is stiff and can rebound, but the hollow bowl shape, rolled rim, and real impacts dissipate energy and risk fracture, so it should not behave as highly bouncy rubber. For collision geometry, a single convex hull is not appropriate because it would close the open top and remove the concave interior. A convex decomposition is recommended for a dynamic rigid body: use multiple hulls around the bowl wall and foot so the interior remains usable while maintaining good PhysX performance. If very accurate interior contact or liquid/particle containment is required, an SDF mesh collider can be substituted at higher cost. Contact offset is kept small at 0.003 m and rest offset at 0.0005 m to avoid visible hovering while still generating stable contacts around the thin rim and foot. CCD is enabled because the bowl has thin ceramic walls and could tunnel through surfaces if dropped or moved quickly. Compliant contacts are effectively disabled with high stiffness and moderate damping because the object is non-deformable; any softness should come from contact stabilization, not material deformation. The center of mass should be close to the vertical central axis and slightly below mid-height due to the heavier lower body and foot ring. Inertia should be computed from the collision decomposition or authored explicitly if high-fidelity tipping behavior is important.
